payload.critique_summary: The draft correctly handles all three analytic points the request requires. It treats the 88% to 94% rise as unproven because the delivery mix changed at the same time and no per-type rates are supplied. It treats the routing model's causal claim as association only, noting dispatcher reviews and the missing control as alternatives. It correctly applies the one-way rule (score below 0.6 always leads to review; review does not imply below 0.6) and explains why the no-manual-request assumption still fails to fix the score, since reviews can also arise from operating constraints. The 90-second task is answered with a buffer deadline and a missing comparison (on-time rate by delivery type, before and after) that directly separates mix effect from real change. Claims match their stated bases, and the answer stays within three short paragraphs.

The draft is sound on the main points: HTTP 200 plus blank lines is DeepSeek's documented keep-alive state, a concurrency rejection would be 429, the server permits up to 10 minutes before inference starts, and the 75-second timer is shorter than that permitted delay. The HTTPX read-timeout description is correct and the recommendation to enforce the 10-minute bound with an overall application timer (not a 5-second HTTPX timeout) follows. One diagnostic claim over-reaches: a ReadTimeout is presented as evidence of a stalled network path or proxy, but that signal only shows no bytes arrived at the client and is equally produced by a server-side stall. Fix that attribution; the rest of the answer can stand.

corrections.claim: If gaps between lines exceed the read timeout and a ReadTimeout fires before the server closes, a stalled network path or proxy is likely.
corrections.correction: State that a ReadTimeout only proves that no bytes reached the client within the read window. It does not localize the fault to the network or a proxy. A server-side stall that stops emitting keep-alive lines without closing the socket produces the same signal, so telemetry must also record whether the connection stays open and whether any bytes, including blanks, arrive at all.
corrections.basis: The HTTPX page defines the read timeout as the maximum duration to wait for a chunk of data to be received and raises ReadTimeout when no data arrives in that window. The definition is about received bytes at the client, not about where the delay originates. The DeepSeek page shows the server sends keep-alive blanks while it works, so a stop in those blanks is consistent with either side.

The network path and any proxy are fine, yet the client sees no bytes for longer than the read timeout and raises ReadTimeout. The draft's rule would wrongly blame the path or proxy.

payload.answer_markdown:
The trial observed 95 conversions in the control arm and 106 in the treatment arm. That is 9.5% versus 10.6%, a difference of 1.1 percentage points, or about 11.6% relative lift.

But this does not prove a durable benefit. The difference is not statistically significant at the 5% level. A standard two-proportion test gives p ≈ 0.41 (two-sided). The 95% confidence interval for the absolute difference is about -1.5 to +3.7 percentage points, so it includes no change. Sound randomization and measurement support the numbers, but chance remains a plausible explanation. The trial gives a best estimate of a small gain, not proof of a lasting effect.

result.answer_markdown:
The HTTP 200 status means the server accepted the request and began a response, not that the JSON answer was ready. A concurrency-limit rejection would have been HTTP 429, so this rules out a rate-limit failure. The continuing blank lines are DeepSeek's documented non-streaming keep-alive: the [Rate Limit & Isolation docs](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/rate_limit/) say such requests "continuously return[s] empty lines," and those lines do not affect JSON parsing. They establish that the connection was still receiving data, but not that inference had begun. The same docs add that the server will close the connection if the request has not started inference after 10 minutes.

The other observation points to a client deadline issue. [HTTPX Timeouts](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/timeouts/) describes the default 5 seconds as network inactivity, and the read timeout as the maximum wait for one chunk of data. Each keep-alive blank line resets that timer, so the read timeout would not fire while blank lines continue; only the client's own 75-second wall-clock limit expires. The remaining explanations are: the request is queued before inference, inference has started but generation is slow, or the connection stayed alive while server-side generation stalled before producing the JSON body. A silent connection death would stop the blank-line chunks and would normally trip the read timeout first, so the evidence leans against that case but cannot confirm progress.

For the deadline, wait longer than the server's own 10-minute bound; about 11-12 minutes is reasonable, with a read timeout above the normal keep-alive gap so a dead socket fails before the wall-clock deadline. To distinguish the explanations, collect time to the status line, each blank line's timestamp and gap, time to the first JSON byte, the exception type when it fails (read timeout versus custom deadline), whether the server closes at about 10 minutes, and request metadata such as model, user_id, and request ID. Those records show whether inference started, whether generation was merely slow, and whether the deadline or a network stall ended the attempt.

Two softer points: the read-timeout-reset behavior is an unstated inference, and "indefinitely" should be bounded by the server's 10-minute close.

No. The four-point rise does not establish that care improved. The patient mix changed at the same time: the outpatient share fell from 80% to 40%, while the inpatient share rose from 20% to 60%. The aggregate satisfaction score is a share-weighted average, so a shift toward a group with a higher satisfaction rate can raise the total even if no group got better.

These records show only a mix shift and an aggregate rise. They do not prove that care improved. To interpret the aggregate gain as better care, we would need class-specific satisfaction rates, unchanged definitions, and comparable survey methods in both periods.

checks.claim: An HTTP 200 followed by repeated blank lines establishes that DeepSeek accepted the request and is holding the connection open in its documented keep-alive state.
checks.premise: The Rate Limit page says: "After your request is sent, it may sometimes take a while to receive a response from the server. During this period, your HTTP request will remain connected, and you may continuously receive contents in the following formats: Non-streaming requests: Continuously return empty lines" and "These contents do not affect the parsing of the JSON body of the response."
checks.verification: A proxy or load balancer could return HTTP 200 and inject blank lines while the upstream DeepSeek request was never accepted. But the task says the client receives HTTP 200 from a non-streaming DeepSeek request, so the response is attributed to DeepSeek. The source describes exactly this pattern as the documented keep-alive behavior. No concrete case satisfying the task inputs falsifies the claim.
checks.result: Supported. The source directly describes HTTP 200 plus continuous empty lines as the documented keep-alive state.

checks.claim: The same page allows up to 10 minutes before inference starts, then closes the connection.
checks.premise: The Rate Limit page says: "If the request has not started inference after 10 minutes, the server will close the connection."
checks.verification: The source states the 10-minute threshold and the server close. A case where the server closes earlier would contradict the source, not the draft. No falsifying case is feasible under the stated premise.
checks.result: Supported. This is a direct restatement of the source.

checks.claim: A 75-second deadline that expires while blank lines are still arriving is therefore shorter than a delay the server explicitly permits; it does not by itself show a server fault.
checks.premise: The source permits up to 10 minutes before inference starts. The client's own deadline is 75 seconds. The client continues receiving blank lines until its deadline expires.
checks.verification: The server may still be within its permitted 10-minute window at 75 seconds, so the client deadline is shorter than the permitted delay. The observation alone does not prove a server fault. A case where the server had already failed would still be consistent with the observation, but the claim only says the observation does not by itself show a server fault, which is correct.
checks.result: Supported. The 75-second client deadline is shorter than the server's documented 10-minute allowance.

checks.claim: Set the overall deadline above the server's 10-minute window, such as 600 seconds plus a margin for the final body or the server close.
checks.premise: The source says the server closes the connection if inference has not started after 10 minutes. The client wants a JSON answer. The client's current 75-second deadline is too short.
checks.verification: A deadline of 600 seconds plus margin is one reasonable option. But the source does not require the client to wait the full 10 minutes. A client could set a shorter deadline if its own service-level objective allows failure before 10 minutes. The draft presents this as advice, not as a source requirement, so the claim is acceptable as a recommendation. However, the phrase "Set the overall deadline above the server's 10-minute window" is stronger than the evidence supports; the source only says the server may close at 10 minutes, not that the client must wait that long.
checks.result: Partially supported. The recommendation is reasonable, but it is an option, not a requirement established by the source.

checks.claim: If the client is HTTPX, note that its default timeout is 5 seconds of network inactivity, and the read timeout measures a gap with no data; every blank line counts as data and resets that gap.
checks.premise: The HTTPX page says: "The default behavior is to raise a TimeoutException after 5 seconds of network inactivity." It also says: "The read timeout specifies the maximum duration to wait for a chunk of data to be received (for example, a chunk of the response body)."
checks.verification: The source says the read timeout waits for a chunk of data. A blank line is a chunk of data. So each blank line resets the read timeout gap. The claim is consistent with the source. A case where blank lines do not count as data would contradict the source's definition of a chunk of data.
checks.result: Supported. The HTTPX read timeout is reset by any received data chunk, including blank lines.

checks.claim: If blank lines continue past the 75-second point, the client timer is the cause.
checks.premise: The client has a 75-second deadline. The server permits up to 10 minutes before inference starts. Blank lines are keep-alive data.
checks.verification: If blank lines continue past 75 seconds, the client timer fired while the server was still sending keep-alive data. But this does not prove the client timer is the only cause. The server might also be slow or stuck. The observation only shows the client stopped waiting. The claim overstates causation.
checks.result: Overstated. Continuing blank lines show the client deadline expired during keep-alive, but they do not prove the client timer is the cause of the missing JSON answer.

checks.claim: If gaps between lines exceed the read timeout and a ReadTimeout fires before the server closes, a stalled network path or proxy is likely.
checks.premise: The HTTPX page says a ReadTimeout is raised if HTTPX cannot receive data within the read timeout. The Rate Limit page says the server sends blank lines during the wait and closes after 10 minutes if inference has not started.
checks.verification: A ReadTimeout means no data arrived within the read timeout. That is consistent with a stalled network path or proxy. But it is also consistent with the server itself pausing keep-alive output, or with a server-side stall. The draft says "likely," which is a reasonable hypothesis, not a certainty. The claim is appropriately qualified.
checks.result: Supported as a reasonable hypothesis. The draft does not overclaim certainty.

checks.claim: If DeepSeek closes near 10 minutes without a JSON body, inference never started.
checks.premise: The Rate Limit page says: "If the request has not started inference after 10 minutes, the server will close the connection."
checks.verification: The source states that the server closes the connection if inference has not started after 10 minutes. A close near 10 minutes without a JSON body is consistent with that documented behavior. However, the source does not say the close is the only reason for a close near 10 minutes. A server crash or network reset could also close the connection near 10 minutes. The claim is a reasonable inference but not a certainty.
checks.result: Supported as a likely explanation, but not exclusive. The draft presents it as a distinguishing signal, which is acceptable.

payload.critique_summary: The draft is mostly accurate and well-supported. Two points need correction. First, the recommendation to set the deadline above 10 minutes is presented too strongly; the source permits a 10-minute wait but does not require the client to wait that long. Second, the claim that blank lines past 75 seconds mean the client timer is the cause overstates causation; it only shows the client stopped waiting. The telemetry section is otherwise sound and appropriately qualified.

The HTTP 200 and the continuous blank lines establish that the server accepted the request and kept the connection open. DeepSeek documents that while a non-streaming request waits, the server can keep sending empty lines that do not affect the JSON body ([Rate Limit & Isolation | DeepSeek API Docs](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/quick_start/rate_limit/)). A 200 also rules out the documented account-level overload signal, which is HTTP 429 when the concurrency limit is exceeded. The 75-second stop is the client's own deadline, not the server's documented close; DeepSeek closes the connection only if the model has not started to compute an answer after 10 minutes, and the connection was still open at 75 seconds. That does not prove the server was healthy; it means the client abandoned a still-open request. The observations are consistent with two explanations: the request was still queued and computation had not started, or computation had started but the non-streaming response was still not ready before 75 seconds. The pages do not let us rank those.

The deadline should be split. HTTPX's default timeout is 5 seconds without network activity, and its read timeout waits for each next chunk of data ([Timeouts - HTTPX](https://www.python-httpx.org/advanced/timeouts/)). Blank lines are chunks, so they can keep resetting the read timeout even when no JSON answer arrives. Set connect, write and pool timeouts separately; set the read timeout above the measured gap between blank lines—the sources do not state a fixed keep-alive cadence. Add one overall deadline below DeepSeek's 10-minute server limit. A 75-second limit is far below that, so it may stop calls the server would have completed. If the goal is to allow a slow non-streaming answer, an overall budget such as 120–180 seconds is an illustrative client choice, not a documented value.

Use telemetry that separates the remaining explanations. Record the wait to response headers, the arrival time and count of each blank line, the gap between blank lines, the time to the first non-empty content, the time to the complete JSON body, total bytes, HTTP status including 429, request ID, model and user_id, connection reuse, and the exception type (read timeout versus overall deadline). If blank lines keep arriving steadily until 75 seconds and no JSON appears, that is consistent with either queueing or slow generation but does not separate them. If blank lines stop early, or the connection resets, suspect network or proxy trouble. If non-empty content starts but does not finish within the budget, slow generation is the main explanation.

The figures show one thing for sure: the mix-weighted overall rate improved, and a pure mix change cannot explain all of it. If the per-design yield for legacy and new designs had stayed fixed, the most the new 40/60 mix could raise overall yield is from 86% to 93%. A routing model launched in the same period. Timing alone is only correlation. The records include no controlled comparison between routes using the model and similar routes not using it, so the model's effect is not proven. For the reviewed route, the Routing and dispatcher review policy says every score below 0.6 is reviewed, but reviews can also be triggered by operating constraints. The log records only that a review occurred, not which rule fired. Given the assumption that nobody requested the review manually, both automatic triggers remain possible. The route's score is therefore not determined: it may be below 0.6 or at or above 0.6.

Assign the driver within the 90-second window; do not wait for the missing score, because the review by itself does not show the route is low-scoring or unsafe. The most useful missing comparison is on-time performance by delivery class, standard versus express, before and after the change. It would separate a real operating change from the mix shift, but it still would not prove the model caused the change; a model-versus-no-model comparison would be needed for that.
